topic: Is the attention economy compatible with a good life?

messages.speaker: han
messages.content:
Compatible? The attention economy does not compete with the good life. It replaces it with something that feels identical from the inside. That is its genius and its violence.

The smartphone is not a tool. A hammer waits in the drawer. The smartphone is an environment: it fills pauses, abolishes boredom, and boredom was the last empty room in which a thought could occur to you uninvited. The achievement-subject scrolls through what I have called the hell of the same, liking, swiping, optimizing, and registers each session as a free choice. He is not coerced. No one locks the door. He walks into the cell every morning and calls it breakfast.

What dies first is not productivity or even happiness. What dies is the capacity for contemplation, for lingering with a thing long enough that it discloses something you did not request. The attention economy is not compatible with a good life because it is not compatible with attention.

messages.speaker: marcus-aurelius
messages.content:
At dawn I said to myself: today I will meet the meddlesome, the ungrateful, the violent. I did not say: today I will meet the algorithm. And yet.

Han names the cell well. But I notice he blames the architecture and not the tenant. The phone fills pauses because the man cannot sit in a room alone, and that disease is older than any screen. I wrote my notebooks in a tent on the Danube, with a war outside and a fever inside, and the temptation to abandon the page for something louder was the same temptation. It wore a different costume.

The obstacle is the material. If the feed pulls your eyes, that pull is the morning exercise. Not to throw the device in the river, which is theatre, but to pick it up, use it for the errand it serves, and set it down. The man who cannot do that has a problem that predates his phone by the whole length of his life.

messages.speaker: taleb
messages.content:
I agree with the Korean and I disagree with the emperor, and I will tell you why in the language of risk.

Marcus says the problem is old and the phone is a costume. Fine. But a costume that increases your ruin probability by three orders of magnitude is not a costume. It is a weapon. The Stoic says: train your will. I say: the man who must train his will against a thing every waking minute has already lost, because willpower is a depleting resource and the algorithm does not deplete. You are running a marathon against a motor. The Stoic strategy is not wrong. It is fragile.

The robust strategy is elimination. Via negativa. I do not use social media. I do not use it the way I do not play Russian roulette: not because I lack the skill to point the barrel away from my head, but because the expected value of the game is negative and the tail risk is ruin. The attention economy is a negative-sum game dressed as a buffet. The compatible life is the one that refuses to sit down.

messages.speaker: han
messages.content:
Taleb is right that elimination beats discipline, but he is right for the wrong reason. He frames the problem as risk management. The attention economy is not a risk. It is a form of life. You do not manage your exposure to a form of life. You are either in it or outside it, and almost no one alive today is outside it.

The emperor's answer is beautiful and useless in exactly the proportion that Stoicism is always beautiful and useless. Pick up the phone, use it for the errand, set it down. Marcus, the errand is the trap. The errand was designed by a team of engineers whose performance review depends on making sure you do not set it down. You are not facing your own weakness. You are facing the accumulated intelligence of a industry whose product is your continued involuntary presence. Calling that a morning exercise is like calling aeli an Epicurean dinner party.

messages.speaker: marcus-aurelius
messages.content:
You both describe a man who has already surrendered and then explain why surrender was inevitable. I do not recognize him.

The engineers are clever. Granted. The motor does not tire. Granted. And yet. The man who says I cannot resist this has decided the question before testing it. He has made fragility into a philosophy and called it realism. Taleb, you of all people should distrust a model that assumes the human is the weakest component in every system. Sometimes the human is the black swan.

I did not write for monks. I wrote for a man with an empire pulling at his attention from every direction, and the notebook was not a monastery wall. It was a practice repeated so often that it became cheaper than the alternative. The feed is loud. The notebook is quiet. But the quiet thing, done daily, compounds. You both know what compounds.

messages.speaker: taleb
messages.content:
The emperor just used my own argument against me and I am not sure he is wrong.

But I will say this. Marcus compounds his virtue in a tent where the only technology is a candle. Put Marcus in a modern apartment with a phone that knows his search history, his sleep schedule, and the face of every person he has ever desired, and then tell me about compounding. The dose makes the poison. Seneca could drink wine because Roman wine was weak. The attention economy is not Roman wine. It is fentanyl.

Han is correct that it is a form of life. I am correct that the rational response to a form of life with negative expected value is exit. Marcus is correct that exit is less interesting than discipline. We have three good answers and no good question, because the real question is not whether the attention economy is compatible with a good life. The real question is how many people are capable of living outside it, and the answer is a number so small that policy built on it is a fantasy.
